speaker: Daniel
text: Welcome, everyone, to today's session on coral reefs and why they matter so much.

speaker: Daniel
text: Reefs look enormous when you swim over them, but they are rare on a global scale.

speaker: Daniel
text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all marine species.

speaker: Daniel
text: That imbalance is exactly why their decline worries biologists.

speaker: Tessa
text: Let me explain what a coral actually is, because it surprises most students.

speaker: Tessa
text: A coral is an animal, a colony of tiny polyps that build a skeleton of limestone.

speaker: Tessa
text: The tiny algae living inside the coral tissue give corals their colour and most of their food.

speaker: Tessa
text: When the water gets too warm, the coral expels those algae and turns white.

speaker: Tessa
text: That is what we call bleaching.

speaker: Tessa
text: A bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving, and the clock is ticking.

speaker: Tessa
text: From a boat, a bleached reef looks almost like snow on the sea bed.

speaker: Tessa
text: Photographs from the air are now one of the fastest ways to map the damage.

speaker: Daniel
text: So how warm is too warm? Less than you might think.

speaker: Daniel
text: Bleaching starts when the water stays about one degree above the usual summer maximum for several weeks.

speaker: Daniel
text: A single hot summer can bleach a reef that is hundreds of years old.

speaker: Daniel
text: Some corals recover if the heat passes quickly, others starve and die.

speaker: Tessa
text: Recovery is possible, and we have watched it happen.

speaker: Tessa
text: After the last major bleaching event, our study reef recovered in about a decade.

speaker: Tessa
text: Fast growing branching corals came back first, and the slow massive corals followed later.

speaker: Tessa
text: But if the hot summers come every few years, there is no time to recover at all.

speaker: Daniel
text: Now a word about the fish, because reefs are not only coral.

speaker: Daniel
text: Parrotfish scrape algae off the rock, and in doing so they grind up coral and produce sand.

speaker: Daniel
text: A large parrotfish can make hundreds of kilograms of sand every year.

speaker: Daniel
text: Many white beaches in the tropics are, quite literally, made by fish.

speaker: Tessa
text: Let me describe how we collect our data.

speaker: Tessa
text: Our dive surveys are done at a depth of fifteen metres, along fixed lines on the reef.

speaker: Tessa
text: Divers photograph every square metre, and software counts the living coral later.

speaker: Tessa
text: We also have sensor buoys that send temperature data every thirty minutes.

speaker: Tessa
text: Tissue samples go back to the lab, where they are stored at minus eighty degrees.

speaker: Daniel
text: Some of you will join the field season next spring.

speaker: Daniel
text: The research vessel is named Albatross, and it sleeps twelve people in rather small cabins.

speaker: Daniel
text: Seasickness tablets are strongly recommended for the first two days.

speaker: Tessa
text: Finally, the assessment.

speaker: Tessa
text: The exam at the end of term will be open book, so focus on understanding rather than memorising.

speaker: Tessa
text: Bring your notes, your field data, and a calculator.

speaker: Daniel
text: That is everything for today, thank you for listening.
